Variants.Content: Located at the eastern end of the Wall, facing the Shivering Sea, Eastwatch is one of the important castles still in use by Night's Watch. It's different from Castle Black and the Shadow Tower: the harbor gives it access to ships, fishing, supplies from the east coast, and views to the northern seas. The Great Wall falls directly into the sea here. Ice, tide and sea wind make the stone walls, piers and sails become part of the defense line. Night's Watch can receive supplies from the south here, and can also observe the coast beyond the wall and distant ships; however, a port never means safety, and bad weather and sea ice often cut off communication before the enemy.
Entry Eastwatch-by-the-Sea Local families also rely on frozen soil, firewood, seal meat, supply convoys and long vigils; if any road, well or dock fails, the price falls first on them.

Entry Eastwatch-by-the-Sea They'll also recognize the accents, laws, and credentials of the Wall; reputations can travel great distances from taverns, and real distances must still be measured by wheel, oar, or horse's hooves.

Entry Eastwatch-by-the-Sea If you can supply supplies, avoid danger, and find a guide, it is worth marking in your itinerary; if you don't have these three things, no matter how loud your family name is, it won't be able to save the lost.

The craftsmen of Eastwatch rely on ship repair wood, canvas, salt, fish catches, and stones to withstand the sea wind to leave behind their craftsmanship, while the clergy use Night's Watch oaths, old gods, and the memory of the dead in the shadow of the Great Wall to explain life and death. A stronghold was therefore not just a lord's hall, but also a place where weddings and funerals, vows, labor and local memories recurred.

Entry Eastwatch-by-the-Sea They care about frozen soil, firewood, seal meat, supply convoys and long vigils. They also look at whether seeds are left after the food collection and whether the city gates are open in times of disaster. When people from afar see the coat of arms, what they see is whether there will be food to eat tomorrow.
